tasks.title: Dry HCl, water and indicators
tasks.prompt: A sealed demonstration has three test conditions: dry HCl passing over dry blue litmus, dry HCl over a moistened strip, and moist air without HCl over a wetted control. Only the second turns red. Explain the three observations in terms of aqueous species, indicator response, and what the controls eliminate.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: The decisive model compares water availability and HCl availability separately. Dry HCl and dry litmus do not form the aqueous environment required for the familiar indicator response. HCl in the wet strip forms hydronium and chloride, enabling acidic response. Moist air without HCl controls for water alone and does not produce the same acidity. The experiment supports medium-dependent indicator chemistry; it does not demonstrate an exact acid concentration.

tasks.title: Dry HCl, water and indicators
tasks.prompt: An unknown solution turns universal indicator red, dry litmus stays blue in a nearby stream of gas, and an aliquot turns blue litmus red after water is added. Compare at least two explanatory models, specify which facts fail to identify the acid species or concentration, and design a two-stage test that would discriminate acid generation from indicator contamination.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: Separate the gas-phase and aqueous observations. A moisture-dependent acid-forming gas is consistent with the dry/wet difference, but indicator contamination or another acid-generating solute may also be possible. Controlled blanks with fresh indicator, measured pH of solvent alone, and an independently chosen species test are required. An indicator colour supports acidity in the tested medium; it does not establish HCl identity, strength, or molarity. Since the species has not been chemically identified, the evidence is underdetermined.

tasks.title: Neutralisation and excess species
tasks.prompt: Mix 15 mL of 0.10 mol/L HCl and 10 mL of 0.10 mol/L NaOH. Draw an initial ion ledger, calculate the acid/base-equivalent remainder, predict the qualitative indicator result, and explain whether NaCl forms a solid under ordinary dilute aqueous conditions.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: HCl contributes 1.5 mmol of acid equivalents; NaOH contributes 1.0 mmol hydroxide. Ion-neutralisation leaves 0.5 mmol H+ equivalent. Na+ and Cl− remain spectators and dissolved NaCl does not precipitate under ordinary conditions. The remaining solution is acidic; initial and final charge balances remain equal.

tasks.title: Neutralisation and excess species
tasks.prompt: A mixture is close to neutral by one indicator and contains unknown acid-derived and base-derived ions; a student infers it must be a solution of pure NaCl. Construct two different reagent combinations compatible with a near-neutral outcome, identify possible salts, and specify what independent measurements would distinguish the models and reveal weak-acid hydrolysis.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: Strong HCl+NaOH can give predominantly NaCl(aq); HCl+KOH gives KCl(aq). Near-neutral indicator colour does not uniquely specify Na+ or K+, nor distinguish all weak acid/base possibilities. Identify ions by suitable verified tests and measure pH quantitatively under controlled conditions; weak acid/base systems can have non-pH-7 equivalence under hydrolysis. The original assertion is not uniquely warranted.

tasks.title: pH, concentration and dilution
tasks.prompt: Two aqueous samples have pH readings 3 and 6 under the same calibrated conditions. After diluting the pH-3 sample with only water, it reads 4. Explain how a higher pH can coexist with unchanged total acid-derived solute amount, and whether the final sample must be neutral.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: pH rose from 3 to 4, consistent with reduced acidity in the diluted aqueous sample. Dilution can reduce concentration/activity without stoichiometrically consuming solute. It need not reach pH 7, and pH alone does not specify total solute amount or the acid species.

tasks.title: pH, concentration and dilution
tasks.prompt: A sample shows pH 3 on a calibrated meter, changes indicator colour after dilution, but a second indicator does not change and a repeat test at different temperature reports another pH. Construct competing explanations and specify which measurements are invariant enough to infer dilution, neutralisation or instrumental error.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: Indicators have distinct transition ranges; a shift can cross one range and not another. pH readings can change with temperature and calibration. Only water was stipulated in dilution, so neutralisation is not established by colour. Verify instruments, temperature and volume changes; test for an added neutralising reagent separately. The observations do not uniquely establish the acid or complete chemical consumption.

tasks.title: Common salts and hydrates
tasks.prompt: A white powder may be NaHCO3 or hydrated Na2CO3. It effervesces with acid; after heating it loses mass. Explain why these observations do not uniquely identify it, and use a charge/atom ledger to design further measurements.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: Both carbonate and hydrogen carbonate species can release CO2 with acid. NaHCO3 can decompose on heating to sodium carbonate, H2O and CO2, whereas hydrated Na2CO3 can lose crystal water. Mass loss and gas release alone need gas identity and dry-residue composition tests. Balance 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3+H2O+CO2, and compare with dehydration of Na2CO3·10H2O.

tasks.title: Common salts and hydrates
tasks.prompt: A laboratory supplies unknown powder A, either sodium hydrogen carbonate, sodium carbonate decahydrate or a mixture. It fizzes with acid and loses mass on gentle heating, but no gas identity or residue composition was measured. Construct at least two incompatible chemical accounts consistent with the observations and specify a sufficient set of follow-up measurements without assuming a pure specimen.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: NaHCO3 can release CO2 and water on heat, while Na2CO3·10H2O can lose hydration water; a mixture can show both. Fizzing on acid addition is compatible with either carbonate-related material. Measure heating-gas identity under controlled conditions, determine anhydrous residue composition, and use stoichiometric mass accounting rather than one colour or mass observation. The current evidence is underdetermined.

tasks.title: Acid reactions and gas identity
tasks.prompt: Two powders release gas with dilute HCl. Gas A turns fresh limewater milky, while gas B does not; zinc and calcium carbonate are candidate starting solids. Write plausible balanced equations, select what gas A could be, and explain why gas B remains unidentified without another test.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: CaCO3+2HCl→CaCl2+H2O+CO2 fits A; Zn+2HCl→ZnCl2+H2 fits a plausible B pathway. Limewater cloudiness supports CO2 under appropriate controls; failure to cloud does not uniquely identify H2. Independent gas confirmation and initial solid identity are needed. Both equations conserve species and charge.

tasks.title: Acid reactions and gas identity
tasks.prompt: An unfamiliar metal-like sample reacts with an unknown acid and produces bubbles; a student declares hydrogen because 'metal + acid always gives H2.' The acid may be oxidising and the solid may contain carbonate contamination. Evaluate at least three chemically distinct gas-generation routes and propose safe supervised discriminating observations.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: Active metal plus dilute nonoxidising acid can form H2; carbonates plus acid form CO2; oxidising acids may lead to nitrogen oxides or other products rather than H2, depending on species/conditions. The starting metal identity, acid identity and contaminant composition remain unknown. One bubble observation is insufficient; controlled reactant analysis and appropriate gas confirmation are needed. No unsafe home test is implied.

tasks.title: Phosphorus oxyacid connectivity (extension)
tasks.prompt: Three structural shorthands are given: H2P(=O)OH, HP(=O)(OH)2 and P(=O)(OH)3. Translate each to molecular formula, count separately O–H and P–H bonds, and predict the acid basicities.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: All have three H atoms in their respective condensed acid formula H3PO2, H3PO3, H3PO4, but contain respectively one, two, three P–OH groups. Their structural basicities in the standard model are 1, 2, 3. P–H hydrogens are not counted as ordinary acid-ionisable O–H protons.

tasks.title: Phosphorus oxyacid connectivity (extension)
tasks.prompt: A student asserts that all H3POx acids are tribasic and that the number of acid-ionisable H also fixes the reducing strength. Use H3PO2, H3PO3 and H3PO4 to separate the two claims, specify one counterexample to each, and explain what additional evidence would be needed for a quantitative redox ranking.
tasks.post_commit_worked_answer: The first claim fails because H3PO2 has only one P–OH and H3PO3 two, despite both formulas beginning H3. The second conflates acid proton donation with redox chemistry: P–H bonds in lower oxyacids are relevant to reducing behaviour, but numerical reducing strength also depends on reaction and conditions. Structure gives qualitative distinctions, not a universal quantitative potential or rate.
